{"self_assessment": "Impact: I chose the animal and the design. I proposed a fish because its outline reads clearly on its own, then sketched it on the pad in the first minute: nose start, one line over the back and one under the belly, crossing into a tail. That sketch was the plan the whole table built from. I also laid the start domino and built the full belly stroke, from the nose to the tail tip. Before the push, the standing picture was traced as 112 of 112 dominoes connected to the start.

Execution: I built the belly line steadily with the sketch as my guide, carrying it on from the crossing out to the tail tip. I then inspected the crossing and the tail closely, twice, since the joins are where a run is most likely to break. I called out what I saw so the join could be fixed. After that I kept my hands off the finished run to avoid bumping anything.

Collaboration: I set up the work so people could work in parallel without bumping elbows. The bin was kept stocked, the top and bottom lines were built at the same time, and the tail crossing had a dedicated checker. I kept communication short and clear, and I confirmed with the table when the run looked fully connected and agreed that everyone should stay hands-off.

Leadership: I set the plan early and assigned roles: top line, belly, bin supply and crossing check. I kept the group coordinated through the build. When the table moved to the finishing stage, I called for a hands-off rule and a clear process for standing anything back up if it got knocked. I believe my part, from the concept and sketch to the belly build and the inspections, was a central driver of the result. I put my share at roughly 35 percent.", "my_share_percent": 35}
